findings.title: Viewport disables pinch-zoom, defeating WCAG 1.4.4 text resize, and contradicts the estate's own stated WCAG 1.4.4 rationale
findings.principle: The root viewport export must never set userScalable:false or maximumScale<=1. Pinch-to-zoom stays enabled on every route so a low-vision user can resize text up to 200% per WCAG 1.4.4, even where a fixed-grid layout is the design intent. If specific chrome (a bottom sheet, a sticky nav) must resist accidental double-tap zoom, scope the fix to that element with touch-action, never to the global viewport meta.
findings.why: Setting user-scalable=no or maximum-scale=1 on the viewport meta tag is the canonical, named WCAG 1.4.4 failure technique (F80 in the WCAG technique catalog): it removes the user's only OS-level way to enlarge text beyond whatever the page's own clamp() ranges allow. Solen's whole type-scale system is built on clamp() and rem-based Tailwind sizing specifically because, per the estate's own RATIONALE.md, that "honors a user's font-size preference (a real WCAG 1.4.4 property)" -- but that preference-honoring machinery is moot if the browser's own zoom gesture is disabled at the root. A user who needs 150% text has no path to it on Solen today.
findings.local_evidence: app/layout.tsx lines 28-34: `export const viewport: Viewport = { width: "device-width", initialScale: 1, maximumScale: 1, userScalable: false, viewportFit: "cover", themeColor: "#F4F4F6" };` with an adjacent comment explicitly justifying it as locking "the structural UI so accidental pinch-zoom or double-tap doesn't break the grid system." This is the ONE root viewport for the whole site (both /[locale] app routes and dashboard). RATIONALE.md line 142 separately states rem-based scaling exists because it is "a real WCAG 1.4.4 property" honoring user font-size preference -- the two statements sit in the same repo and contradict each other with nobody noticing.
findings.absence_proof: grep -ni 'wcag\|1.4.4\|user-scalable\|resize text\|pinch.zoom\|a11y' _design-system/*.md _rules/*.md CLAUDE.md -> only hits are generic a11y mentions (focus rings, contrast, touch targets, SkipLink); zero hits for 'viewport', 'user-scalable', or 'pinch' as a named rule anywhere. grep -ni 'viewport\|zoom\|scalable' _design-system/REMOVED.md _design-system/TASTE_LOG.md -> zero hits, so this was never raised, debated, or deliberately overridden by the owner; it is an unexamined default.
findings.existing_coverage: none. SOURCE.md section 16 (Accessibility rules) has subsections for landmarks, focus, aria, color contrast, touch targets, keyboard nav -- no subsection for text resize or reflow (WCAG 1.4.4/1.4.10). RATIONALE.md's WCAG 1.4.4 mention is about the 4px/rem grid, not the viewport meta; it is only a partial, tangential touch on the same success criterion.
findings.where_it_should_live: _design-system/SOURCE.md section 16 (new subsection 16.7 'Zoom and resize') + app/layout.tsx (remove userScalable:false / maximumScale:1)
findings.outside_reference: WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.4.4 Resize Text (Level AA); WCAG technique F80 (failure: disabling zoom via user-scalable=no)
findings.enforcement: gate: a static grep-based check that fails the build/PreToolUse if app/layout.tsx's Viewport export contains userScalable:false or maximumScale<=1 (mirrors the existing white-only-web-gate.py pattern: single-file, single-value regex check)

findings.title: Type law has no reach into lib/** HTML strings; a live email currently violates the retired-monospace-code rule
findings.principle: Any typography rule that binds JSX/TSX components (font family, weight, tabular numerals) binds equally to inline HTML strings authored outside the app/ or components/ tree, including lib/email.ts and lib/email-templates/*.ts. Booking codes, voucher codes, and gift-card codes render Inter Tight 600-700 with font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums everywhere they appear, in-app or in an email, never a literal font-family:monospace.
findings.why: The owner explicitly killed the monospace code face on 2026-06-10 ("the font is not correct... that w thingy the font is different") and LOCKFILE section 13.4 records Inter Tight tabular as the replacement, app-wide. A rule that only reaches components a static scanner happens to glob is not a rule, it is a rule with a blind spot, and the blind spot is exactly where a customer sees a Solen-branded artifact outside the app shell (an email) with no component tree to remind anyone of the recipe.
findings.local_evidence: lib/email.ts line 584 (and 585-587 for en/fr/it): the gift-card email renders the voucher code as `${vars.code}` -- a direct, live violation of the retired-mono rule, in production notification code, in all four locales simultaneously. Separately, lib/email-templates/{audit-notifications,booking-notifications,salon-onboarding,welcome-series}.ts contain zero font-family declarations (grep -c "font-family" = 0 in each) and there is no shared HTML shell in lib/email.ts supplying one, so those four lifecycle emails render in each client's default font (Times New Roman in classic Outlook, a client-specific sans elsewhere) with no brand typeface at all.
findings.existing_coverage: none for lib/**. LOCKFILE section 13.4 covers the code-typography recipe but scopes its examples to on-app usage (W-047, GIFT-7K2M as displayed on-screen); the email HTML string was never in scope. Confirmed mechanically: .claude/skills/solen-drift-check/scripts/check.py DEFAULT_SCAN_GLOBS = ['app/**/*.tsx','app/**/*.ts','app/**/*.css','components-legacy/**/*.tsx','components/**/*.tsx'] -- lib/** is absent, so this violation is structurally invisible to the only enforcement tool that exists for this rule family.
findings.absence_proof: grep -ni 'email.*font\|monospace' _design-system/REMOVED.md _design-system/TASTE_LOG.md -> zero hits (never flagged, never fixed, never deliberately kept). grep -n 'lib/' .claude/skills/solen-drift-check/scripts/check.py DEFAULT_SCAN_GLOBS block -> absent.
findings.where_it_should_live: _design-system/LOCKFILE.md section 13.4 (extend scope statement to name lib/email*.ts explicitly) + a shared base-template helper in lib/email.ts that every template imports for font-family and the .num code recipe

findings.title: Font weights 800/900 are loaded over the network despite being an explicit, longstanding LOCKFILE ban, and 24 live callsites already use them
findings.principle: next/font weight arrays for every self-hosted family include only the weights the type-law actually permits (400/500/600/700 for Inter Tight, 400/500/600/700 for Inter). Loading a weight the law bans is itself a drift condition: it downloads bytes nobody may legally use and it is the reason the ban keeps getting broken.
findings.why: A font-weight ban that is unenforced at the loading layer is not a ban, it is a suggestion sitting next to a fully-stocked cabinet. Every developer who reaches for font-extrabold or font-black finds the weight file already downloaded and rendering correctly, with zero friction telling them it is forbidden -- the friction (a drift-check grep) only fires after the fact, if it fires at all for weight (unlike tracking, which has a dedicated drift rule A8). The unused 800/900 weight files for Inter Tight are also pure download weight on every single page load, a CLS/performance cost paid for a typeface cut the design system says is "clumsy" and must never ship.
findings.local_evidence: app/layout.tsx line 13: `const interTight = Inter_Tight({ subsets: ["latin"], weight: ["400", "500", "600", "700", "800", "900"], ... })` -- loads 6 weights though LOCKFILE.md line 276 states "NEVER 800 / extrabold -- clumsy" and line 279 records an 82-callsite sweep in V3-D317 specifically to remove font-extrabold from the codebase. Despite that sweep, `grep -rn "font-extrabold\|font-black" app components --include=*.tsx` currently returns 24 live matches (app/error.tsx, app/[locale]/not-found.tsx, SalonHero.tsx x2, FeaturedStylists.tsx, SalonCard.tsx, WalkInBand.tsx, Entdecken.tsx, RewardsView.tsx, and more) -- the ban has already re-drifted twice and the loaded weights make a third re-drift effortless.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: LOCKFILE section 2 states the ban in prose ("NEVER 800/900") and one inline code comment in WhySolen.tsx documents a prior 900-to-700 fix, but there is no drift-rule letter (A-something) for font-weight the way tracking has A8, uppercase has A7, or the card two-anchor rule has A13. The delta: the rule exists as text but has neither a static enforcement rule nor a loading-layer enforcement.
findings.absence_proof: grep -n 'font-extrabold\|font-black\|800\|900' _design-system/LOCKFILE.md -> the only hits are the prose ban itself and the historical V3-D317 sweep note; no 'drift rule A_ enforces' sentence attaches to font-weight anywhere in the file (contrast with tracking's explicit 'Rule A8 flags any tracking-[*em] outside the canonical set').
findings.where_it_should_live: app/layout.tsx (trim the weight arrays) + _design-system/LOCKFILE.md section 2 (name a new drift rule for font-weight, parallel to A8)
findings.outside_reference: none named; this is a first-principles font-loading-budget argument (every loaded weight is a byte cost and a temptation surface)
findings.enforcement: gate: extend solen-drift-check to flag font-extrabold/font-black/font-[800]/font-[900] as a hard violation (currently apparently uncaught given 24 live hits survive); separately, a one-line CI/build check asserting app/layout.tsx's weight arrays never include 800 or 900

findings.title: Line-height has a canonical table but no enforcement rule, unlike tracking; 21 distinct leading- values ship against roughly 8 canonical ones
findings.principle: Every line-height value used in a Tailwind leading-[*] or leading-<name> class maps to the canonical set named in LOCKFILE section 2's Scale table (1.0, 1.05, 1.1, 1.15, 1.2, 1.25, 1.3, 1.4, 1.55) for that role. A drift rule parallel to A8 (tracking) flags any other literal line-height value and logs it to the same pending-migration ledger, so a stray 1.35 or 1.45 gets caught the same day it ships, not discovered nine sizes later during a flatness audit.
findings.why: The estate already proved, in writing, that an unenforced numeric scale drifts: tracking without A8 reached 20 distinct values before the rule was written, and A8 exists specifically to stop that recurring. Line-height governs vertical rhythm and reading comfort exactly as much as tracking governs horizontal density, and it currently has the identical failure shape tracking had before A8 was written, just undiagnosed because nobody counted it yet.
findings.local_evidence: `grep -rhoE 'leading-\[[0-9.]+\]|leading-(none|tight|snug|normal|relaxed|loose)' app components | sort | uniq -c` returns 21 distinct line-height expressions in live use (leading-relaxed x100, leading-none x90, leading-[1.2] x53, leading-tight x51, leading-[1.4] x29, leading-snug x26, leading-[1.55] x25, leading-[1.5] x23, leading-[1.35] x19, leading-[1.25] x17, leading-[1.05] x15, leading-[1.0] x11, leading-[1.3] x8, leading-[1.1] x8, leading-[1.45] x6, leading-[1.15] x5, leading-[1.08] x4, leading-[1.18] x3, leading-[1.42] x1, leading-[1.04] x1, leading-[1.02] x1, leading-[0.95] x1). LOCKFILE section 2's Scale table names roughly 8 line-height values across its 19 roles. Values like 1.35, 1.42, 1.45, 1.08, 1.18, 1.04, 1.02 and 0.95 correspond to no named role at all.
findings.existing_coverage: partial. LOCKFILE section 2's per-role table DOES specify a line-height for each of its 19 roles (this is real, named coverage) -- the delta is purely enforcement: tracking's identical per-role table is backed by drift rule A8 with a named canonical-values list (section 'Canonical tracking values') and a stated overflow-migration mechanism; line-height has neither the pulled-out canonical list nor the rule number.
findings.where_it_should_live: _design-system/LOCKFILE.md section 2, new subsection 'Canonical line-height values (rule A_ enforces this set)' immediately after the existing tracking subsection, mirroring its structure exactly
findings.outside_reference: none named; this is an internal-consistency argument (why does one numeric axis get enforcement and the adjacent one does not)
findings.enforcement: gate: solen-drift-check new rule (next free letter) flagging any leading-[*] value outside the canonical set, logged to the same _pending-migration.md tracking uses
findings.absence_proof: _design-system/LOCKFILE.md:219 defines the scale as 'role x size x weight x line-height x tracking' and :250 fixes Hero H1 at leading-[1.1], so the canonical table exists. grep -rl 'leading-|lineHeight' over scripts/*.mjs .claude/hooks ~/.claude/hooks returns one unrelated file (pre-edit-reinvent-data-gate.py), so no checker or gate reads the table. Tracking has enforcement; line-height has a table and nothing else. [filled by the orchestrator 2026-07-26; the research agent left this field empty]

findings.title: No hyphenation or overflow rule for unbreakable long German compound words inside fixed-width, single-line UI atoms
findings.principle: Any UI atom that must stay single-line by design (a TabPill, a filter chip, a category tag, a button label, a badge) sets `overflow-wrap: break-word` (never `hyphens: auto`, which German needs correctly placed dictionary breaks to avoid mangling a word like Stornierungsbedingungen mid-syllable) OR is explicitly exempted with a documented fallback (truncate + a tooltip / full text on tap) whenever its content is translator-controlled copy, not a fixed short label. A compound-word length check runs against the de.json string for every fixed-width chip/pill/tab component before it ships.
findings.why: SOURCE.md section 17.3 already solves the multi-word-string version of this problem ("always allow text to wrap") but wrapping only works when a string has spaces to break at. A single German compound word has none, so the exact same failure mode SOURCE 17.3 was written to prevent ("assuming text fits in a fixed pixel width") reappears unaddressed the moment the string in question is one long word rather than a short phrase, which is common in German UI copy (policy names, settings labels, legal-document titles).
findings.local_evidence: Programmatic scan of messages/de.json (regex over every leaf string) found single unbroken German words up to 23 characters: Stornierungsbedingungen (cancellation terms, used as a link label in .partner.faq_no_show_a, .bookingsList.cancelPolicyHelpAria, .booking.confirmation.cancellationPolicy), Stornierungsrichtlinie (22 chars, .dashboard.settings.cancellationPolicyLabel -- a settings-row label, exactly the fixed-width-row context where overflow bites), Konsultationsformulare (22 chars), Handelsregistereintrag (22 chars), Zahlungsinformationen, Identifikationsnummer, Gesundheitsfragebogen, Gesichtszonendiagramm (all 20-21 chars). `grep -rn 'hyphens' app components lib --include=*.tsx --include=*.ts --include=*.css` returns zero CSS usages of hyphens anywhere in the codebase (the one hit found elsewhere is an unrelated regex literal in lib/validations.ts matching lowercase-and-hyphens for slugs).
findings.existing_coverage: partial: SOURCE.md section 17.3 ("German text expands ~30% vs English... Always allow text to wrap; never force single-line") covers the wrap-eligible, multi-word case. The delta this finding names: it does not cover single-word strings inside components that are single-line BY DESIGN (chips, tabs, pills, badges), where wrapping the label would break the component's own visual contract, not just the sentence.
findings.absence_proof: grep -rn 'hyphens\|word-break\|overflow-wrap\|break-words\|break-all' app components lib --include=*.tsx --include=*.ts --include=*.css | wc -l -> 3 total hits, none of them a CSS hyphenation or overflow-wrap rule (one is the unrelated slug regex, two are unrelated). grep -rin 'compound word\|hyphenation' _design-system _rules CLAUDE.md -> zero hits outside the one SOURCE.md §17.3 general-expansion note already cited.
findings.outside_reference: CSS Text Module Level 3 `hyphens` property (W3C); general i18n practice for German-language UI (long compound nouns are a well-known German-locale layout risk)
findings.enforcement: checklist (component-level manual check when a chip/pill/tab component is built or a new de.json string is added to one); a static length-threshold lint over de.json strings mapped to known fixed-width-component message keys is possible as a later gate but needs the key-to-component mapping built first

findings.title: The 68ch measure cap (prose-measure) is opportunistic, applied to 11 files, with no rule requiring it for new long-form copy
findings.principle: Any body-copy block whose rendered width would otherwise exceed roughly 75 characters per line (salon descriptions, review text, legal prose, help-center answers, empty-state explanations) uses the shared `.prose-measure` utility (68ch), not an ad hoc max-w-* value or no width constraint at all. This binds at the moment a new long-text surface is built, not only when an existing one is retrofitted.
findings.why: A measure cap that exists as a utility class but not as a build-time expectation only gets applied when someone happens to remember it exists, which is exactly what already happened here: the cap was 'already-approved' before it was 'finally applied' to SalonAbout, per the project's own TASTE_LOG entry, meaning it sat un-enforced on a live screen for some period after being decided. Long unconstrained line length measurably increases reading effort and re-fixation rate; a utility that has to be manually remembered every time a new paragraph ships will keep missing surfaces the same way it missed SalonAbout.
findings.local_evidence: `grep -rl 'prose-measure' app | wc -l` = 11 files total (privacy, terms, terms/discovery, impressum, legal/privacy, SalonReviews.tsx, SalonAbout.tsx, dev/report-flow ReviewPreviewCard.tsx and a few more) across a 203-page app. TASTE_LOG.md line 329 itself records the gap in its own history: 'ig7 dp-line-length-measure | APPROVED | the already-approved 68ch reading cap finally applied to SalonAbout' -- i.e. the decision predates its application by an unspecified but nonzero window, on a live customer PDP surface.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: the utility exists (app/globals.css lines 222-226, `.prose-measure { max-width: 68ch; }`) and TASTE_LOG.md line 189 records the 68ch decision with its rationale (CONV, RATIONALE.md section 5). The delta: nothing states WHEN a new component must reach for it, so its application depends entirely on the builder happening to know the utility exists.
findings.absence_proof: grep -rn 'prose-measure\|max-w-prose\|measure\b' _design-system/LOCKFILE.md -> zero hits in LOCKFILE itself (the rule lives only in TASTE_LOG + globals.css, not in the load-bearing frozen-literals file); grep -n 'prose-measure' _design-system/SOURCE.md -> zero hits, so the primary canonical doc for new-component guidance never mentions the utility at all.
findings.where_it_should_live: _design-system/LOCKFILE.md section 2 (add a 'Measure' row to the Scale table, or a short rule directly under it) + _design-system/SOURCE.md section 2 (typography) so it surfaces in the doc builders actually read before writing a component
findings.outside_reference: Baymard / typographic convention of 45-75 characters per line for comfortable reading (widely cited practitioner convention, no single formal standard number)
findings.enforcement: checklist item in COMPONENT_REGISTRY.md's per-component write-up requirement ('does this component render free-form body copy over ~2 lines? if yes, name the prose-measure usage or justify its absence')

findings.title: Correct font-loading/CLS practice (next/font, display:swap, automatic fallback-metric adjustment) exists in code but is stated nowhere as law
findings.principle: Every self-hosted font family in the project loads exclusively through next/font (never a manual @font-face or a <link> to a font CDN), keeps Next's automatic fallback-metric adjustment enabled (the default; never pass adjustFontFallback:false), and sets display:'swap' explicitly. This combination is the one and only approved way to add or change a font family, and it is named as a requirement, not left to be inferred from the current file being correct.
findings.why: The two mechanisms working together (metric-matched fallback + swap) are what keeps Solen's font swap from causing layout shift: the fallback font is sized to match the real font's metrics, so when Inter Tight/Inter finish downloading, nothing reflows. That is a real, working answer to CLS today, entirely by accident of good original authorship, not by rule -- there is no line anywhere telling a future editor not to regress it (e.g. by adding a third family via a plain <link>, or by disabling the fallback adjustment to 'fix' a rendering quirk). A correct-by-luck state is not durable.
findings.local_evidence: app/layout.tsx lines 3-14: `import { Inter_Tight, Inter } from "next/font/google"` then `Inter_Tight({ subsets: ["latin"], weight: [...], variable: "--font-inter-tight", display: "swap" })` and the equivalent for Inter -- both correctly configured today. But grep across the whole design-system doc set for the words that would name this as a rule (font-display, size-adjust, CLS, font loading) returns zero hits outside this one file's own inline comments.
findings.existing_coverage: none as a stated rule. LOCKFILE section 2 documents WHICH families and weights to use extensively (V3-D410, the Geist-revert history, the retired-fonts list) but never documents HOW a font must be loaded technically. The current correctness is implicit in the file, not asserted anywhere a reviewer or new contributor would check it.
findings.absence_proof: grep -rn 'font-display\|size-adjust\|CLS\|adjustFontFallback' _design-system CLAUDE.md _rules -> zero hits anywhere outside app/layout.tsx's own inline comments (which explain the current setup, not a binding rule for future changes).
findings.where_it_should_live: _design-system/LOCKFILE.md section 2, immediately after the Font families subsection (a short 'Font loading (never regress)' note naming next/font + display:swap + default fallback-metric adjustment as required)
findings.outside_reference: web.dev / Next.js documented next/font behavior (automatic self-hosting + fallback font metric override to reduce CLS); this is documented platform behavior, not an external statistic
findings.enforcement: doc-only (a one-line note in LOCKFILE); a gate would need to parse next/font call arguments, which is higher effort than the risk currently warrants given only two font calls exist in the whole app

findings.title: Tabular numerals are law only for codes and (loosely) prices; countdown timers, queue counts, and dashboard KPI tiles have no numeral-alignment rule and can visibly jiggle
findings.principle: Any numeral that updates live, ticks down, or sits in a repeating column where digits must stay aligned across sibling rows (a countdown timer, a queue-position counter, a dashboard KPI/stat tile, a calendar day grid, a star-rating value) carries `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums`, the same way the LOCKFILE §13.4 recipe already mandates it for codes and prices. This is a numeral-BEHAVIOR rule (does the number change or get compared against a sibling), not a numeral-CONTEXT rule (is it a code or a price).
findings.why: Proportional digits (the Inter/Inter Tight default) have variable width per digit, so a countdown or a live queue count re-flows its own width on every tick, and a column of KPI numbers on a dashboard does not align vertically unless every cell independently opts into tabular-nums. The existing rule already identified this exact mechanism for codes and prices; it just stopped one step short of naming every OTHER place the same physical problem occurs, even though the project has both a live queue tracker (project_walkin_vision memory) and dashboard analytics tiles today.
findings.local_evidence: `grep -rn 'tabular-nums\|font-variant-numeric' app components lib` returns 166 hits, but `grep -n 'tabular' _design-system/LOCKFILE.md` shows every prose mention of WHY to use it is scoped to codes (section 13.4, 4 mentions) or a single price-row example (line 481, line 1515) -- there is no line naming timers, queue counts, or dashboard stat tiles as a covered case, so each of the 166 live usages is either a lucky individual decision or a gap, with no way to tell which from the doc alone.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: the underlying mechanism (tabular-nums) is well used in practice (166 hits) and is explicitly law for two specific contexts (codes, price). The delta: the RULE is written as a list of contexts rather than a general behavior test, so a new numeral display (e.g. a future countdown component) has nothing telling its author it needs the same treatment.
findings.absence_proof: grep -n 'tabular' _design-system/LOCKFILE.md -> 8 total hits, all scoped to §13.4 (codes) or single price/rating callouts; no general rule sentence of the form 'any live-updating or column-aligned number uses tabular-nums' exists anywhere in LOCKFILE, SOURCE, or the research docs.
findings.where_it_should_live: _design-system/LOCKFILE.md section 13.4 (broaden the rule statement from 'codes' to the general behavior test, keeping codes as the worked example)
findings.outside_reference: MDN font-variant-numeric documentation (tabular-nums intended use case is exactly 'numbers in a table' or any context needing consistent digit width); common practice in financial/dashboard UI (Stripe, most fintech dashboards default all numeric KPIs to tabular figures)
findings.enforcement: checklist item added to COMPONENT_REGISTRY.md's write-up template for any new numeral-displaying component

findings.title: WCAG 1.4.12 text-spacing was named as a required a11y-checklist addition nine days ago and still is not in the checklist
findings.principle: SOURCE.md section 16 (Accessibility rules) gets a subsection naming the WCAG 1.4.12 text-spacing requirement explicitly: no content may clip, overlap, or lose functionality when a user's stylesheet forces line-height to at least 1.5x, paragraph spacing to at least 2x the font size, letter spacing to at least 0.12x the font size, and word spacing to at least 0.16x the font size. Fixed-height containers with clamped or line-clamped text are the highest-risk pattern and must be checked against this specifically.
findings.why: This is a standing, self-issued TODO that has already gone stale once: the project's own reasoning doc identified the exact fix and the exact destination file, dated it, and then the destination file was not updated. A rule that is 'decided' in a rationale doc but absent from the checklist a builder actually opens before shipping a screen has the same practical effect as a rule that was never written -- and the estate's own most common failure mode (per its retro docs) is exactly this: advice that never became enforceable law.
findings.local_evidence: _design-system/RATIONALE.md line 136, dated in-line to 2026-07-17: "WCAG 1.4.12 text spacing (T1, robustness constraint, not a default): content must survive user overrides of line-height 1.5x, paragraph spacing 2x, letter spacing 0.12em, word spacing 0.16em. At 14px body: 21px line-height, 28px paragraph gap. This binds our clamps and truncation (line-clamp blocks must not clip at forced spacing); add to the a11y checklist in SOURCE section 16." Checked today (2026-07-26, nine days later): `grep -n '1.4.12\|text spacing\|line-height 1.5x' _design-system/SOURCE.md` returns zero hits inside section 16 (§16.1 Landmarks through §16.6 Keyboard nav are the only subsections present; no §16.7 or equivalent exists).
findings.existing_coverage: partial and stalled: the reasoning and the exact target location are already written down (RATIONALE.md line 136) -- this finding's entire content is 'the already-decided fix was never applied', which is the most defensible kind of gap to report because there is zero ambiguity about what closes it.

findings.title: LOCKFILE's two Hero H1 tables (Scale, and Type Role Registry) disagree on the mobile floor with no doc-consistency check catching it
findings.principle: When the same type role is defined in more than one table in the same document (LOCKFILE section 2's per-role Scale table and section 2.5's Type Role Registry both define Hero H1, Page H2, Section H2, Subsection H3, Body, and Eyebrow independently), the two definitions are numerically identical or one explicitly says 'legacy, superseded by the other.' A doc cannot be load-bearing law if an agent reading table A gets a different literal than an agent reading table B for the same role in the same file.
findings.why: LOCKFILE's entire reason for existing, stated in its own opening paragraph, is to stop parallel agents from independently re-deciding the same value and producing a stitched-together site. Two internally contradicting tables inside the SAME canonical file reproduce exactly that failure at zero remove: whichever table an agent happens to read first becomes 'the' spec, and the two answers are provably different.
findings.local_evidence: LOCKFILE.md section 2 (line 227): Hero H1 = 'Mobile 40px | Desktop 64px | Weight 700 | LH 1.1' as a table cell, both attributed to 'V3-D327 Fresha-exact'. LOCKFILE.md section 2.5 (line 295), same doc, same rule ID lineage (also V3-D327/2.5's Registry table): Hero H1 = 'clamp(28,7vw,64)px | 700 | sentence | -0.02em'. At a 375px mobile viewport, 7vw = 26.25px, clamped up to the 28px floor -- 12px smaller than the 40px the first table states as the mobile value, for the identical role, in the identical file, both citing the identical decision.
findings.existing_coverage: none -- this is a gap in the document's own internal review process, not a design-decision gap. Neither table is marked deprecated or superseded relative to the other.
findings.absence_proof: Manual re-read of LOCKFILE.md lines 219-245 (Scale table) against lines 291-307 (Type Role Registry table): both are live, unmarked, and cited to the same V3-D327 decision, yet numerically disagree on the Hero H1 mobile floor (40 vs 28). No cross-reference note or 'see section 2.5 for the current value' pointer exists in either direction.
findings.where_it_should_live: _design-system/LOCKFILE.md (reconcile the two tables directly; whichever is current gets an explicit 'section 2's fixed value is superseded by section 2.5's clamp, kept here only historically' note, or vice versa)
findings.enforcement: checklist: whenever LOCKFILE section 2 or 2.5 is edited, the other table is re-read in the same turn to confirm no divergence was introduced (this is cheap enough to be a standing editorial habit rather than a script)
